title: Quoting an interval
objectives: Give a 90% range for an unknown quantity, and score ranges by width and hit rate.

screens.title: Nine times in ten
screens.prose: An interviewer asks for a range you are 90% sure holds the answer. Your belief is normal, centred on 50 with an sd of 10. Slide the half-width until the shading holds 0.90.
screens.question: Where does the upper end sit?

hints.text: Watch the probability label as you slide.
With the ends at 40 and 60 it holds only 0.68.
The ends sit 16.45 either side: 33.55 to 66.45.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the label reads 0.90.

byKey.two: That is 2 sd, which holds 0.95. A 90% range is a little narrower.
byKey.one: That is 1 sd, which holds only 0.68.

explain.text: A 90% range leaves 5% in each tail. For a normal belief that is $1.645$ sd either side: 33.55 to 66.45. Nine times in ten the truth should land inside.

screens.title: The 1.645 rule
screens.prose: For a normal belief the 90% range is the mean $\pm 1.645$ sd. A new belief: mean 200, sd 30.
screens.question: What is the lower end of the 90% range? Give 2 places.

hints.text: Multiply the sd by 1.645.

explain.text: $1.645 \times 30 = 49.35$, so the range is 150.65 to 249.35. The multiplier fixes the share held; the sd fixes the width. A wider belief means a wider range, never a different multiplier.

screens.title: Scoring a range
screens.prose: A range from $l$ to $u$ scores its width, plus 20 times any distance by which the truth falls outside. Lower is better. Asked for the sum of 1 to 100, a candidate says 4,000 to 6,000.
screens.question: The sum is 5,050. What does the range score?

widget.accept: 2,000: a hit, so the score is the width, 6,000 − 4,000.
widget.label: Score

hints.text: Is 5,050 inside the range?
It is a hit, so no miss penalty.
The score is the width: $6{,}000 - 4{,}000 = 2{,}000$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A hit scores its width alone.

byKey.zero: You scored a hit as 0. A hit still pays for its width.
byKey.centre: You scored the distance from the centre. Only a miss adds distance.

explain.text: The range holds 5,050, so it scores its width, 2,000. A range of 5,000 to 5,100 would also hit and score 100. Width is the price of safety.

screens.title: The range game
screens.prose: The interviewer treats your range as a quote: bid at the low end, ask at the high end, for 20. If the truth is above your ask they buy; below your bid they sell. A miss costs 20 times its distance. Width is capped at 10.
screens.question: Finish both turns without losing money, and no rule breaks.

schedule.text: How many primes are there below 100? Quote your 90% range: bid at the low end, ask at the high end, for 20. A width of 10 at most.
A hint: there are 15 primes below 50, and primes thin out as numbers grow.

hints.text: How many primes are there below 50? How fast do they thin out?
15 below 50; fewer than 15 more are likely between 50 and 100.
A range of 18 to 28, then 20 to 30 after the hint, holds the answer.

feedback.correct: Your ranges held the answer both times.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A range that misses is traded against at the wrong end.

byKey.low: The truth fell outside a range, and the interviewer traded 20 against you. Centre nearer the count and use the width.
byKey.crossed: Your low end met or passed your high end. A range needs a low end below the high one.
byKey.spread: Your width left 2 to 10. A range wider than 10 says too little; under 2 is a point guess.

explain.text: There are 25 primes below 100. The model ranges 18 to 28 and 20 to 30 both hold 25, so nobody traded. The opening 30 to 40 misses by 5 and is sold 20 at 30 twice: −£200.

screens.title: What a miss costs
screens.prose: The interviewer's trades left you at £{{carry.range.pnl|0}}. Each £20 lost is one unit of miss distance. The truth is 25.

state.caption: The model run, and the opening range for one turn

screens.question: On one turn at 30 to 40, the interviewer sells you 20 at 30. What is that trade's P&L at the truth 25?

hints.text: You bought 20 at 30. What is each worth?
Each is worth 25.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. You bought 20 at 30, each worth 25.

byKey.sign: You bought above the truth, so the trade loses.
byKey.width: That is both turns. One turn costs 100.

explain.text: You bought 20 at 30 something worth 25: −£100. That is 20 times the miss of 5, the miss part of the score. Two turns at that range cost £200.

screens.title: The whole score
screens.prose: Now score the range 30 to 40 itself, on the truth 25, with width and miss together.
screens.question: What does 30 to 40 score?

hints.text: Score is width plus 20 times the miss.
Width 10, miss $30 - 25 = 5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the width to 20 times the miss.

byKey.width: You scored the width alone. The range missed by 5.
byKey.miss: You scored the miss alone. Add the width, 10.
byKey.five: You added the miss without its weight of 20.

explain.text: $10 + 20 \times 5 = 110$, against a score of 10 for a range that held 25. The weight of 20 makes a miss expensive. It equals $2/\alpha$ for a 90% range, with $\alpha = 0.1$.

screens.title: Six out of ten
screens.prose: A candidate gives ten 90% ranges and six of them hold the truth. If their ranges were calibrated, each would hit with chance 0.9, independently.
screens.question: For a calibrated candidate, what is the chance of 9 or more hits? Give 4 places.

hints.text: Add the chances of exactly 9 and exactly 10.
Exactly 9 is $10 \times 0.9^9 \times 0.1 = 0.3874$; the sum is 0.7361.

byKey.ten: That is exactly 10 alone. Add exactly 9.
byKey.nine: That is exactly 9 alone. Add exactly 10.

explain.text: A calibrated candidate scores 9 or 10 hits 73.6% of the time. Six or fewer happens with chance only 0.0128. Six hits is strong evidence the ranges are too narrow.

screens.title: Too sure
screens.prose: After six hits in ten, the candidate says: "My ranges were sharp. Narrow ranges show confidence."
screens.question: What should they change?

options.text: Widen the ranges until about nine in ten hold
Narrow them further, to look more confident
options.why: You traded calibration for looks. Each miss costs 20 times its distance.

options.text: Nothing: six is just bad luck
options.why: You blamed luck. A calibrated candidate scores six or fewer only 1.3% of the time.

options.text: Quote 0 to a million every time
options.why: You made the range say nothing. Its width alone then scores a million.

hints.text: How often should a 90% range miss?
One time in ten. These missed four in ten.
Widen until the hit rate is near nine in ten.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The ranges missed far more than one time in ten.

byKey.narrower: You traded calibration for looks. Each miss costs 20 times its distance.
byKey.luck: You blamed luck. A calibrated candidate scores six or fewer only 1.3% of the time.

explain.text: Candidates often give ranges that are too narrow; six or seven hits in ten is a common report. The fix is wider ranges, not braver ones. A range that says nothing fails the other way.

screens.title: Powers of ten
screens.prose: Some quantities span powers of ten, such as shares traded on an exchange in a day. Work in logs. If your best guess is $10^9$, good to half a power of ten, the range is $10^{8.5}$ to $10^{9.5}$.

state.caption: The axis is $\log_{10}$ of the count

screens.question: What is the upper end, in billions? Give 2 places.

hints.text: So the upper end is 3.16 billion and the lower end 0.316 billion.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Half a power of ten is a factor of $\sqrt{10}$.

byKey.linear: You added half a billion. In logs, half a power of ten multiplies by 3.16.
byKey.ten: That is a whole power of ten above. The range is half a power each side.

explain.text: The range is 316 million to 3.16 billion, symmetric in logs and lopsided in counts. A count also cannot be negative, so a symmetric range in counts would be wrong. Choose the scale on which your doubt is symmetric.

screens.title: The interval score
screens.prose:
For a 90% range, $\alpha = 0.1$, and a range from $l$ to $u$ on the truth $x$ scores
$$S = (u - l) + \frac{2}{\alpha}(l - x)^+ + \frac{2}{\alpha}(x - u)^+.$$
The best range reports your true 5% and 95% points.
screens.question: A range 20 to 24 on a truth of 25. What does it score?

hints.text: Width first, then the miss.
Width 4; the truth is 1 above the top.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Width 4 plus 20 times the miss of 1.

byKey.width: You scored the width alone. The range missed by 1.
byKey.noweight: You added the miss without its weight of 20.

explain.text: Width 4 plus a miss of 1 at weight 20 gives 24. The narrow range loses to a range of 10 that hits. The score rewards honest 5% and 95% points, no tighter.

screens.title: Ranges in code
screens.prose: Code the score, the hit rate and the normal range. `NormalDist` from `statistics` gives the 1.645.
screens.question: Complete `interval_score`, `hit_rate` and `normal_range`.

widget.starter:
from statistics import NormalDist


def interval_score(lo, hi, truth, alpha=0.1):
    """Width plus 2/alpha times any miss distance."""
    ...


def hit_rate(ranges, truths):
    """Share of (lo, hi) ranges that hold their truth."""
    ...


def normal_range(mean, sd, level=0.9):
    """(lo, hi) holding level of a normal belief,
    rounded to 2 places."""
    ...
widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. A truth on an end counts as a hit. Normal ranges are rounded to 2 places.

hints.text: A miss below is `max(0, lo - truth)`; above is `max(0, truth - hi)`.
A 90% range leaves 5% each side: `inv_cdf(0.95)`.
For a general level use `inv_cdf(0.5 + level / 2)`.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the weight $2/\alpha$ and the two-sided quantile.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that each `...` is replaced.

explain.text: The weight is $2/\alpha$, so a 95% range would weigh misses at 40. `inv_cdf(0.95)` is 1.645 and `inv_cdf(0.975)` is 1.96. The hit rate over many ranges is your calibration check.

screens.title: A morning range
screens.prose: A trader's battery often has an intervals paper, and desks do the same each morning. The free guide *Probability and Markets*, written by a trading firm about its interviews, treats ranges this way. Your belief for today's close: mean £102.40, sd £1.20.
screens.question: What is the low end of your 90% range for the close, in pounds? Give 2 places.

hints.text: Use the mean less 1.645 sd.

explain.text: The range is £100.43 to £104.37. Over a month, the close should land outside it on about two days. More misses mean the sd was set too low.

ideas: A 90% range should hold the truth nine times in ten: for a normal belief, the mean $\pm 1.645$ sd.
Score a range by its width plus 20 times any miss; lower is better.
Six hits in ten says the ranges are too narrow: a calibrated set does that only 1.3% of the time.

formula.name: Interval score at 90%
formula.note: $x$ is the truth; the 20 is $2/\alpha$ with $\alpha = 0.1$.

summary.trap: Ranges far too narrow to look confident: each miss costs 20 times its distance.

quiz.question: What is the upper end of the 90% range?

explain.text: $1.645 \times 100 = 164.5$, so the range is 835.5 to 1,164.5. The multiplier is the same for every normal belief. Only the sd scales it.

quiz.prose: Asked for $7!$, a candidate gives 3,000 to 4,000. The answer is 5,040.
quiz.question: What does the range score?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Width plus 20 times the miss.

byKey.width: You scored the width alone. The range missed by 1,040.

explain.text: The miss is $5{,}040 - 4{,}000 = 1{,}040$, weighted 20: 20,800. Add the width for 21,800. A range of 4,000 to 6,000 would have scored 2,000.

quiz.question: How many ranges hold their truth?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A truth on an end counts as a hit.

byKey.ends: You left out truths that sit on an end, such as 4 in (3, 4). Those are hits.

explain.text: The misses are 25 in (10, 20), 61 in (50, 60) and 4 in (5, 15). The other seven hold, including the ends 4, 2 and 40. Seven in ten is below the nine a calibrated set expects.

quiz.prose: You are asked for a 90% range on the number of complaints a broker gets in a quiet week. Your best guess is 2.
quiz.question: Which range is most sensible?

options.why: You made it symmetric. A count cannot be negative, so the low end stops at 0.
You gave a point. A count this small varies a lot week to week.
You made it say nothing. Its width alone scores 1,000.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A count has a hard bound at 0.

byKey.sym: You made it symmetric. A count cannot be negative, so the low end stops at 0.

explain.text: A count cannot go below 0, so the range is lopsided. The upper end stretches further than the lower one. Ranges follow the shape of your doubt, not a template.
